beats.say: The CIA once tried to turn a cat into a spy. With a microphone inside it. That's not a theory. It's in their own files.
Four conspiracy theories that sounded crazy, and turned out to be true. Counting down to the biggest one, the one the CIA tried to shred. That one's at the end.
And I'll be honest. I'm a meatball. Everyone already thinks I'm hiding something. It's sauce. I'm hiding sauce.
Comment your guess before I tell you. Which one of these actually helped start a war? The spy cat? The ship attack? The fake attack plan? Or the mind control? Lock it in.

beats.say: I'm Meatball, by the way. I investigate weird stuff, and I tell you what's actually true. Subscribe. A new case every Tuesday and Saturday.
Number four. The nineteen sixties. The CIA has a problem. It wants to listen to private conversations, and people keep noticing the guy with the microphone.
beats.chapter: Acoustic Kitty: the CIA spy cat

beats.say: But nobody notices a cat. So the plan was simple. Put the microphone inside the cat.
Inside the agency, the project got a name. Acoustic Kitty. Which, to be fair, is a great name.
A microphone in its ear. A transmitter at the base of its skull. An antenna woven through its tail.
As a meatball, I would also like to object to this. Nobody is putting an antenna in me. I don't even have a tail.
Here's the catch. Cats do not take orders. In training, it kept wandering off whenever it got hungry.
They kept trying anyway. The project took years of work, and one estimate put the cost at twenty million dollars. For a cat.
One former CIA officer later claimed that on its first real test, it was hit by a taxi. Other accounts say the cat lived. Either way, the mission went nowhere.
In 2001, a declassified CIA memo called the idea not practical. So: spy cat, real. Spy cat that works? Not so much.
And that was the cute one. Number three helped start a war.
Number three. August nineteen sixty-four. An American destroyer, the USS Maddox, is patrolling off the coast of North Vietnam.

shots.photo: Torpedo launchers from the Gulf of Tonkin gunboat, 1964

beats.say: On August second, North Vietnamese torpedo boats really did attack it. That part is true. This bullet hit the ship.

shots.photo: Bullet that struck the USS Maddox, 2 Aug 1964 (Navy museum)

beats.say: Two nights later, in a storm, the crews reported a second attack. Torpedoes in the water. Radar contacts everywhere.

shots.photo: Torpedo launchers from the Gulf of Tonkin gunboat, 1964

beats.say: Within days, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, and America's war in Vietnam grew fast.
The vote wasn't close. Four hundred sixteen to zero in the House. Eighty-eight to two in the Senate.
That same night, before anyone checked, the President went on TV and announced air strikes.
But the destroyer's own commander had already sent a message saying the reports looked doubtful, and asking for a full review before anyone acted.

shots.photo: Torpedo launchers from the Gulf of Tonkin gunboat, 1964

beats.say: Here's the twist. The second attack almost certainly never happened.
In 2005, the National Security Agency released its own historian's study. It found no attack that night, and that the intercepts had been presented as proof when they weren't.

shots.photo: Bullet that struck the USS Maddox, 2 Aug 1964 (Navy museum)

beats.say: I've been attacked by a radar ghost too. It was a fork. It was just a fork.
And remember the one the CIA tried to shred? We're getting closer. Stick around for it.
So that's how the guess comes out. The ship attack helped start a war. And number two is worse. Number two was planned on purpose.
If this is the weirdest thing you've learned today, hit like. It helps more people find Meatball.
Number two. March nineteen sixty-two. America's top generals send a memo to the Secretary of Defense.
Its title: Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba. The idea: invent reasons to start a war.
Stage attacks on the US base at Guantanamo. Blow up an American ship and blame Cuba.
Sink a boat of Cuban refugees, real or simulated, and blame that too. And if John Glenn's space launch failed, blame Cuba for that as well.
It even suggested holding funerals for fake victims, so the newspapers would print them. Fake victims. Real funerals. Someone typed that.
Even fake the shooting down of a passenger plane, by swapping it for an empty drone.
The memo was signed by the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Lyman Lemnitzer.

shots.obs: wm:GEN Lyman L. Lemnitzer, portrait as SACEUR (cropped 2).jpg

beats.say: For the record, I have never planned a fake anything. I'm a real meatball. Fully real. Look at me.
Here's the good news. President Kennedy's administration said no. None of it happened.

shots.obs: wm:President Kennedy American University Commencement Address June 10, 1963.jpg

beats.say: We only know because the memo was declassified in nineteen ninety-seven, and published in two thousand one.
So that's a plan that never happened. Number one did happen. For twenty years.
Number one. Project MKUltra. Nineteen fifty-three. The Cold War. The CIA is afraid its enemies have learned to control minds.
CIA director Allen Dulles approves a secret research program. For twenty years, the CIA pays for experiments at universities, hospitals and prisons, often through fake front groups.
There were about a hundred and fifty separate sub-projects. Some were run out of apartments in San Francisco and New York, where people were secretly given drugs.
They tested drugs, including LSD, plus hypnosis and sleep deprivation. Sometimes on people who never agreed to it, or never even knew.
This part isn't funny, so I won't joke. Real people were hurt, and some lived with it for the rest of their lives.
Then, in nineteen seventy-five, a presidential commission and Senate investigators started asking questions.
In nineteen seventy-three, the CIA director ordered the MKUltra files destroyed.
Here's the twist. They missed some. In nineteen seventy-seven, about twenty thousand documents turned up, misfiled in a records center.
That same year, the US Senate held public hearings. It's all on the record now.
So, four conspiracy theories, all true. A spy cat, an attack that didn't happen, a fake war plan, and a mind control program.
But look at how we know. Every one came out through documents, investigations and records you can read yourself.
That's the test. Most theories never pass it. These four did. Which is exactly why I check.
And for every theory like these, there are dozens that fall apart the second you check. I'll investigate those too. Out loud. With stamps.
So, were you right? Which one helped start a war? Tell me in the comments.
